title: Thinking under check
objectives: Learn a reliable order to check your options when in check
Practice blocking a check and following up
Practice converting a material advantage into checkmate

steps.text: There are only ever three ways to answer a check — capture the checking piece, block the line of attack, or move your king to safety. Working through them in that order, every time, keeps you from missing your best option under pressure.

steps.prompt: Tap the three responses to check in the order you should try them, strongest option first.
steps.successExplanation: Capturing removes the threat completely, so try it first. Blocking only works against a sliding piece, and only if a square between it and your king is empty. Moving the king is the fallback — it's legal whenever the other two aren't.

steps.text: Let's put 'block the check' into practice. White is in check from the rook on e8. There's no way to capture it, so the knight has to block the line — then be ready for what happens next.

steps.prompt: Block the rook's check with your knight, then continue after Black recaptures.

steps.text: One last idea before you finish this off: with a rook and king against a lone king, keep your rook a full move away from the black king so it can't be attacked, and use it to fence the black king onto fewer and fewer squares along a rank or file. Bring your own king up to help — the black king can't cross a line your rook is guarding. Once it's pinned to the very edge of the board, a rook check along that edge is checkmate.

steps.objective: Checkmate the lone black king using your rook and king — fence it toward the edge, then deliver mate along that edge.

steps.summary: Capture, block, or move — in that order, every time you're in check. And when the position is winning, remember checkmate is the goal, not just winning material: fence the lone king to the edge with your rook, then deliver mate there.
